abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet current therapeutic strategies lack sustained efficacy and long-term stability. Our study aimed to construct a humanized rodent model for drugs development especially currently prevalent small interfering RNA medication.
METHODS: A humanized hypertensive mouse model was generated by subcutaneous injection of neonatal mice with adeno-associated viruses encoding hAGT (human angiotensinogen) and hRENIN (human renin). Blood pressure was monitored weekly via tail-cuff plethysmography. Expression of hAGT and hRENIN was assessed by ELISA, Western blot, and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography at 4 and 6 months postinjection. Hypertension-associated comorbidities were examined through histological analysis and ELISA. A modified N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA targeting human hepatic AGT (GalNAc-siAGT) was screened and subcutaneously administered to humanized hypertensive mice, either alone or in combination with valsartan, to evaluate therapeutic efficacy.
RESULTS: The dual adeno-associated virus-induced humanized hypertensive model exhibited a sustained hypertension for 6 months and manifested prevalent comorbidities, including heart failure and kidney disease. This modified GalNAc-siAGT demonstrated significant activity in knocking down hAGT both in vitro and in vivo. Only a single subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siAGT in humanized hypertensive mice led to a sustained reduction in blood pressure lasting for 2 months, accompanied by cardio- and renoprotective effects. Moreover, combining GalNAc-siAGT with the renin-angiotensin system blocker, valsartan, significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study validated the antihypertensive therapeutic effect of GalNAc-siAGT in a humanized hypertensive murine model while highlighting the translational potential of this model for clinical drug development.

abstract:
The purpose of this study is to assess the safety profile of intramuscular injections of the Acne mRNA vaccine at 3 dose levels compared with placebo in 12 to 17 years old participants with moderate to severe acne.

An early safety data review (ESDR) will be conducted after each subcohort has completed an injection round; enrollment of the next higher dose level subcohort or progression of a subcohort to the subsequent injection round will only proceed if no safety concerns are identified. This sequential process will allow a cautious approach to vaccine injection in the adolescent population.

Study details are as follows:

* Before being enrolled in the study, participants complete a 4-week (ie, 1-month) screening period during which they will be called over the telephone approximately in the middle of the screening period to check they are not using prohibited medications and to remind them about the facial hygiene requirements.
* Once the screening period has been completed, the study duration will be up to 13 months for each participant
* Participants will be invited to a long-term extension study through a separate protocol.

abstract: The therapeutic potential of CRISPR/Cas genome editing has advanced the development of precision medicine; however, its clinical translation for many in vivo applications remains limited by challenges in achieving safe, efficient, and targeted delivery. Conventional viral vectors and synthetic nanocarriers are associated with challenges including immunogenicity, limited cargo capacity, prolonged nuclease expression, off-target effects, and manufacturing complexities. Engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being investigated as alternative delivery carriers due to their biological origin, capacity for cargo encapsulation, and opportunities for surface functionalization. However, their biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers depend on vesicle source, formulation, and experimental conditions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design of engineered EVs for CRISPR/Cas delivery, with a particular focus on strategies to improve cargo loading, targeting specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different CRISPR cargo formats, including plasmid DNA, mRNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, together with endogenous and exogenous loading approaches, hybrid EV platforms, and methods for enhancing intracellular delivery. Advances in EV surface engineering through genetic, chemical, physical, and biomimetic modifications are highlighted as strategies being investigated to improve tissue-specific delivery and functional cargo transport. The review also highlights emerging research directions, including CRISPR-EV theranostic platforms and the application of artificial intelligence to enhance CRISPR-EV therapeutic systems. Finally, key translational challenges, including scalable production, EV heterogeneity, cargo-loading efficiency, biodistribution, regulatory standardization, and quality control, are critically discussed. EV-mediated CRISPR delivery remains at an early preclinical stage, with clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy yet to be established. Further advances in EV engineering, cargo-loading strategies, and manufacturing standardization are needed to support its potential clinical translation.

abstract: Targeted reduction of hepatic antithrombin (AT) via siRNA offers a promising strategy to enhance thrombin (TMB) generation in bleeding disorders, though efficient hepatocyte delivery remains challenging. This study developed and evaluated a targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation incorporating a novel morpholine-based ionizable lipid (MIL) and a lactobionic-octadecylamine conjugate (LBN) for hepatocyte-specific delivery of AT-siRNA (siAT). Following synthesis of MIL and LBN, siAT-loaded LNP (siAT LNP LBN) were prepared using microfluidics and characterized for size, morphology, zeta potential, polydispersity index, and encapsulation efficiency (EE). Functional assays on HepG2 cells assessed cellular uptake, protein knockdown, and AT activity. The optimized formulation exhibited uniform particles (124 nm, PDI 0.125, zeta potential - 8.9 mV) and high EE (90%). Cytotoxicity assays confirmed safety up to 65 pmol siRNA. LBN-decorated LNP significantly enhanced hepatocyte uptake compared to non-targeted LNP and naked siRNA. Optimal AT mRNA suppression occurred at ~ 65 pmol siRNA and 16 h, with protein knockdown confirmed at 48 h. Functionally, siAT LNP LBN reduced AT activity to 48.1 ± 5.5%, substantially outperforming non-targeted LNP (64.1%) and naked siRNA (86.6%). The developed siAT-LNP-LBN platform demonstrated efficient hepatocyte uptake, robust AT knockdown, and low cytotoxicity in vitro, providing preliminary evidence for its potential as a hepatocyte-targeted siRNA delivery platform. Further in vivo studies are warranted to evaluate its biodistribution, liver-targeting efficiency, pharmacodynamic effects, therapeutic efficacy, and biosafety.

title: Targeted siRNA-lactobionic lipid nanoparticles with novel ionizable lipid inhibit antithrombin III expression in hepatocytes.

abstract: Delivery formulations that facilitate mRNA transfection in the respiratory system aim to provide a flexible platform to address or prevent respiratory disease in a patient-accessible, targeted manner. Recent clinical trials in cystic fibrosis, respiratory oncology, and mucosal vaccination have exposed the unique physicochemical and immunological challenges that differentiate respiratory and parenteral mRNA strategies. This review examines the nanomaterials, barriers, and experimental models central to the rational development of aerosolized mRNA medicines. We begin with an overview of the most promising classes of devices and nanomaterial formulations used for respiratory delivery. We then analyze the physical barriers to nasal and lung delivery, spanning delivery-associated physical stresses and anatomical matrices, and present the major chemical and biological strategies developed to overcome them. A parallel analysis addresses the immunological barriers of the respiratory mucosa, including the innate and adaptive cell populations and the sensing pathways that mRNA delivery engages. Immunoengineering approaches to improve the tolerability of repeat dosing are discussed, including nucleoside modification and alternative RNA constructs, degradable and anti-inflammatory material chemistries, and co-administration of standard-of-care pulmonary drugs. Finally, we address methodologies for the investigation of the nanomaterial-mucosal interface using biophysical characterization techniques, and evaluate preclinical models spanning in vitro mucus mimics, air-liquid interface cultures, ex vivo precision-cut lung slices, in vivo rodent and non-rodent species, three-dimensional (3D) nasal and lung cast replicas, and mathematical models of the intranasal airways and lung. We propose an interdisciplinary bioengineering approach that combines the expertise of chemists, immunologists, and pulmonologists to enable clinical translation of respiratory mRNA medicines.

title: From aerosol to alveoli: materials, methods, and models to bridge barriers to respiratory delivery of RNA.

abstract: Precision engineering of CRISPR/Cas9 components has advanced genome editing toward therapeutic applications. Fully chemically modified guide RNAs (gRNAs) have the potential to improve stability and broaden therapeutic delivery strategies. However, extensive chemical modification of CRISPR guides can compromise genome editing activity by disrupting gRNA-Cas9 interactions. Here, we employed an iterative, structure-guided optimization strategy to systematically evaluate chemical modifications throughout SpyCas9 gRNAs. Extending beyond commonly used nucleotide modifications, we incorporated 2'-amino-RNA, 4'-thio-RNA, and extended nucleic acid (exNA) to generate gRNAs in which 90%-100% of nucleotides are sugar- or backbone-modified. Although the performance of individual modification patterns varied among target sequences, we established a repertoire of guides that support robust genome editing in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings provide a systematic framework for rational engineering of heavily and fully modified gRNAs using diverse nucleotide chemistries for nonviral CRISPR genome editing.

abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells have emerged as promising candidates for adoptive immunotherapies. Their natural cytotoxic capabilities and low incidence of side-effects such as cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity, render NK cells a favorable alternative to T cells. Incorporation of a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) has been shown to greatly enhance NK cell's antitumor capacity. Nevertheless, CAR-NK cell therapies still face several challenges, such as low in vivo persistence, low tumor homing of the transfused cells and the effects of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Genetic modifications of key cellular mediators show great potential to overcome these hurdles. While well-established viral engineering strategies are currently the most commonly used techniques, biosafety concerns, high costs, and labour-intensive protocols have encouraged innovation toward nonviral strategies. In this review, we describe recently established viral and nonviral technologies used for NK cell engineering, focusing on their respective advantages and disadvantages. In addition, we highlight the most important functional refinements and mechanistic characterizations of NK cells and genetically optimized NK cells in the context of the TME and how these advances can be progressed toward therapeutic translation.

title: Killers by Design: How Innovative Gene-Engineering Fine-Tunes NK Cells as Next Generation Immunotherapies.

abstract: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive motor neuron loss. Aberrant RNA metabolism is one of its most consistent molecular features, and ALS has long been framed as a disease of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), given that mutations in RBPs are among the most frequent genetic causes of ALS. However, a growing number of ALS-associated genes encode proteins that lack canonical RNA-binding domains; nonetheless, their mutations also disrupt RNA homeostasis. This review examines how these non-canonical disease modulators perturb RNA metabolism. We group these factors into three functional classes. One includes proteostasis regulators, whose dysfunction impairs protein quality control and promotes the accumulation of aggregation-prone RBPs in cytoplasmic inclusions and persistent stress granules. Another involves factors that elicit RNA toxicity or disrupt ribonucleoprotein organization, including GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9ORF72 and CAG repeat expansion in ATXN1. The third class comprises factors governing axonal RNA granule transport. Across these categories, a shared consequence is the disruption of mRNA processing, stability, localization, and translation in motor neurons. We further discuss how epitranscriptomic dysregulation, particularly altered m6A and m1A modification states, may contribute to ALS pathology. We also discuss the therapeutic implications of this mechanistic convergence in defective RNA metabolism in ALS.

abstract: Previously, we used an aminooxy click chemistry (AOCC) strategy to introduce pairs of ligands into oligonucleotides during solid-phase synthesis by using nucleoside and non-nucleoside building blocks. However, the standard oligonucleotide synthesis conditions were incompatible with the incorporation of certain complex ligands. In this report, first, a post-oligonucleotide synthesis solution-phase AOCC approach was developed to address this issue. Different pairs of ligands were conjugated to oligonucleotides through an O-amino building block incorporated during the solid-phase synthesis. Second, a small interfering RNA with a sense strand conjugated using the AOCC strategy to target the ApoB gene using a receptor-targeting ligand (GalNAc) and a pharmacokinetic enhancer (C16 alkyl) was evaluated in mice. The bis-heteroconjugate had a longer duration of action and higher level of silencing than the siRNA carrying only the receptor-targeting ligand.

abstract:
The purpose of this study is to learn about the safety and effects of updated COVID-19 vaccines (called BNT162b2) in participants 5 Through 64 Years of Age with risk factors for Severe COVID-19, and Participants 65 Years of Age and Older.

This study is seeking participants who:

* are medically stable
* have not had a recent COVID-19 infection or a recent COVID-19 vaccination
* have not received certain routine vaccines recently
* participants that are 5 through 64 years of age will need to have at least 1 medical condition that increase their risk of complications from COVID-19.

Participants in Cohort 1 of this study will receive a single age-appropriate dose (30 mcg for participants aged ≥12 years; 10 mcg for participants aged 5-11 years) of BNT162b2 vaccine 1 which targets COVID-19 (2026/2027 recommended strain) injected in the upper arm. The study team and participants will know which injection they receive.

Participants in Cohort 2 of this study will randomly receive 1 injection into their upper arm of either: BNT162b2 vaccine 1; BNT162b2 vaccine 2, or BNT162b2 vaccine 3 which targets COVID-19. The study team and participants will not know which injection they receive.

Participants enrolled in Cohort 1 will be in the study for about 2 months and will have at least 3 scheduled visits. Participants enrolled in Cohort 2 will be in the study for about 6 months and will have at least 3 scheduled visits. Participants will record side effects and complete diaries following visit procedures. For Cohort 1 the study team will collect a nose swab and blood samples at 2 of the 3 visits. For Cohort 2 the study team will collect a nose swab and blood samples at all of the visits.

abstract: Hypodematium angustifolium, a fern species endemic to Korea, has no reported genomic characteristics or phylogenetic position. In this study, the complete chloroplast genome of H. angustifolium was assembled and characterized: 150,022 bp in length with a typical quadripartite structure. Overall, 128 genes were identified (87 protein-coding genes (PCGs), eight ribosomal RNAs, and 33 transfer RNAs). Additionally, 73 RNA editing sites were predicted. Phylogenetic analysis based on 84 PCGs showed that H. angustifolium was clearly distinguishable from H. crenatum. These genomic data provide a resource for future phylogenetic and evolutionary studies of Hypodematium.

abstract: C9ORF72 is involved in multiple neuronal functions and a major factor in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, a fatal neurodegenerative disease. Pathogenicity is implemented through an intronic repeat expansion in the gene's mRNA leader that produces long, repetitive RNA and dipeptides when translated through repeat associated non-canonical translation. The expanded repeat also suppresses transcription of the major transcript variant (Variant 2) which comprises 90% of the C9ORF72 levels in healthy cells, leading to an additional loss-of-function effect. Examining the sequence, structure, and ribosome occupancy of Variant 2's mRNA leader in detail, we found that translation of C9ORF72 is tightly regulated through a multi-layered system. To deconvolute this system, we conducted a mutant screen and developed a method to evaluate the results quantitatively. We found that near-cognate start codons in all three frames, a start-stop element in frame 2, a uTranslon in frame 1, and secondary structures cooperate to keep baseline C9ORF72 translation low. Further, initiation at upstream near-cognate start codons reduces the impact of both the start-stop and the uTranslon, effectively buffering their repressive function and creating a feedforward loop. A strong secondary structure in the Variant 2-specific sequence further modulates initiation at all the elements. We hypothesize that this buffered repressor system has evolved to ensure reliable, noise-insensitive expression of this critical regulator of neuronal function. Finally, we used ADAR-based RNA editing of specific sites in Variant 2's mRNA leader, increasing translation of the gene and providing a novel avenue to rescue the loss-of-function phenotype in disease.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have rapidly emerged as a transformative approach for treating a range of health challenges. Accelerated by the success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, this platform holds promise beyond immunisation for the transient expression of therapeutic proteins in targeted tissues. Despite this promise, non-invasive delivery of mRNA-encoded cargo to the brain remains a challenge, as most peptide drugs do not pass the blood-brain barrier. Here, we present the development of an intranasal mRNA-LNP therapeutic that drives production of neurotrophic factors in the nasal epithelium and delivery of the encoded protein to the brain. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that intranasal delivery of mRNA encoding the neurogenic factor BDNF (Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor) enhances memory performance in both aged mice and a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. This approach offers a promising platform for delivering therapeutic proteins to the brain and opens new avenues for treating age-related and neurodegenerative disorders.

abstract: This phase II trial studies how well trametinib works in increasing tumoral iodine incorporation in patients with thyroid cancer that has come back or spread to another place in the body. Trametinib may stop the growth of tumor cells by blocking some of the enzymes needed for cell growth and may help make treatment with iodine I-131 more effective.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing radioiodine (RAI) activity by determining the proportion of patients alive at 6 months without disease progression by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST version \[v\]1.1) criteria following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort A) II. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the objective response rate (ORR) at 6 months following treatment with radioiodine (RAI) in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort A) III. To determine the proportion of patients following trametinib therapy with increased tumoral iodine incorporation as quantified by iodine iodine-124 (I-124) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) lesional dosimetry. (Cohort B)

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine the proportion of patients following trametinib therapy with increased tumoral iodine incorporation as quantified with I-124 PET/CT lesional dosimetry. (Cohort A) II. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib with or without RAI. (Cohort A) III. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with RAI. (Cohort A) IV. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort A) V. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the ORR at 6 months following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort B) VI. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the proportion of patients alive at 6 months without disease progression by RECIST v 1.1 criteria following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort B) VII. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib with or without RAI. (Cohort B) VIII. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with RAI. (Cohort B) IX. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort B) X. Preliminary evaluation of best objective response (BOR) rate for patients treated with trametinib alone. (Exploratory) (Cohort C) XI. Preliminary evaluation of the proportion of patients following treatment with trametinib alive at 6 months without disease progression by RECIST v 1.1 criteria. (exploratory) (Cohort C) XII. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib. (Cohort C) XIII. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with trametinib. (Cohort C) XIV. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort C) XV. To explore the impact of continued trametinib upon RAI avidity and efficacy. (Exploratory) (Cohort C)

OUTLINE: Patients with RAS gene mutations are assigned to Cohort A, while patients without BRAF/RAS gene mutations are assigned to Cohort B.

COHORT A: Patients undergo iodine I-124 PET/CT on day 5 of week 1. Beginning day 6, patients receive trametinib orally (PO) daily for 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo second iodine I-124 PET/CT on week 5. If I-124 PET/CT shows enough iodine absorption, patients may receive iodine I-131 PO and continue receiving trametinib for another 2 days. If I-124 shows that the thyroid is not absorbing iodine, patients have the option to be assigned to Cohort C.

COHORT B: Patients undergo iodine I-124 PET/CT on day 5 of week 1. Beginning day 6, patients receive trametinib PO daily for 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo second iodine I-124 PET/CT on week 5. If I-124 PET/CT shows enough iodine absorption, patients may receive iodine I-131 PO and continue receiving trametinib for another 2 days. If I-124 shows that the thyroid is not absorbing iodine, patients have the option to be assigned to Cohort C.

COHORT C: Patients may continue trametinib at the doctor's discretion and do not receive iodine I-131.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up for 30 days.

abstract: This randomized phase II trial studies the safety of and how well aspirin works in preventing Barrett's esophagus from returning after it has been successfully eliminated by radiofrequency ablation. Studying samples of tissue from patients with Barrett's esophagus for the levels of a specific protein that is linked to developing Barrett's esophagus may help doctors learn whether aspirin can prevent it from returning after it has been successfully treated.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To conduct a randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled phase II chemoprevention trial, investigating whether supplementation with aspirin 325 mg/day for 12 months is safe and reduces the expression of CDX2 messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) (a biomarker which has been associated with the risk of developing Barrett's esophagus \[BE\]) in comparison to placebo after successful radiofrequency ablation (RFA).

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To assess safety at 12 months. II. To assess differences in the expression of CDX2 at 18 months, activation status of NF-kB by assessing levels of total and phosphorylated (phospho)-p65 and cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation of phospho-p65 which is likely to be affected by aspirin.

III. To assess the prostanoid marker, prostaglandin E2, and prostaglandin synthases, which are known to respond to aspirin and to correlation with clinicopathological factors in the esophageal cancer.

IV. To assess differences in the expression of proinflammatory cytokines known to induce activation of NFkB, i.e., TNFalpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17A, IL-23 will be measured.

OUTLINE: Patients are randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

ARM A: Patients receive aspirin orally (PO) once daily (QD) for 12 months.

ARM B: Patients receive placebo PO QD for 12 months.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, and 18 months.

abstract: This phase IIA trial compares the effect of acolbifene versus low dose tamoxifen in preventing breast cancer in premenopausal women at high risk for developing breast cancer. The usual approach for patients at increased risk for breast cancer is to undergo yearly breast magnetic resonance imaging or ultrasound in addition to yearly mammogram. Premenopausal women at very high lifetime risk for breast cancer (greater than 50%) can consider preventive removal (mastectomy) of both breasts. Premenopausal women age 35 or older with a prior diagnosis of atypical hyperplasia, lobular carcinoma in situ, or an estimated 10-year risk of greater than or equal to 3% or estimated 10-year risk of greater than or equal to 2-5 times that of the average woman (depending on age) may be advised to consider five years of standard dose tamoxifen. Standard dose tamoxifen is four times the dose used in this study. Estrogen can cause the development and growth of breast cancer cells. Acolbifene and tamoxifen blocks the use of estrogen by breast cells. This study may help researchers measure the effects of acolbifene and low dose tamoxifen on markers of breast cancer risk in mammogram imaging, breast tissue, and in blood samples.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if there is a difference in change in expression of the endocrine resistance gene anterior gradient 2 (AGR2) in benign breast tissue of premenopausal women at increased risk for breast cancer randomized to acolbifene 20 mg versus (vs) tamoxifen 5 mg orally daily for 6 months.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine if there is significant within-arm effect of 6 months of acolbifene 20 mg or tamoxifen 5 mg as assessed on the Estrogen Response Gene Index (ERGI) in benign breast tissue.

II. To determine if there is significant within-arm effect of 6 months of acolbifene 20 mg or tamoxifen 5 mg on mammographic density as measured by change in fibroglandular volume (FGV) and mammographic percent dense volume.

III. To determine if there is a significant within-arm effect of 6 months of acolbifene 20 mg or tamoxifen 5 mg on Menopause-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (MENQOL) or Hot Flash Score.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. Assess within arm change in breast epithelial cell protein expression of Ki-67 in specimens with \>= 2% baseline Ki-67.

II. Assess within arm change in bioavailable serum estradiol, testosterone, progesterone.

III. Association of baseline anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) (\>= 1 ng/ml associated with normal ovarian reserve) with 6-month serum estradiol and change in tissue estrogen responsive gene expression (ERGI and AGR2).

IV. Association of tamoxifen and acolbifene parent drug and active metabolite levels with change in tissue estrogen response genes and mammographic density.

V. Assess within arm change of AGR2, Forkhead box protein A1 (FOXA1), estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) proteins on residual fixed specimens acquired by random periareolar fine needle aspiration (RPFNA) and processed to blocks.

VI. Assess within arm change in metabolic measures including triglycerides, measures of insulin sensitivity and thyroid binding globulin (Kansas University Medical Center \[KUMC\] participants only).

OUTLINE: Patients are randomized to 1 of 2 groups.

GROUP I: Patients receive acolbifene orally (PO) once daily (QD) for 6 months in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients also undergo three-dimensional (3D) mammography and collection of blood samples during screening and at the end of acolbifene treatment. In addition, patients undergo RPFNA during screening and on day 1-10 of their menstrual cycle, or if not menstruating, at the convenience of the patient and study staff.

GROUP II: Patients receive tamoxifen PO QD for 6 months in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients also undergo 3D mammography and collection of blood samples during screening and at the end of tamoxifen treatment. In addition, patients undergo RPFNA during screening and day 1-10 of their menstrual cycle, or if not menstruating, at the convenience of the patient and study staff.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up between 21-35 days.

abstract: Encapsulation efficiency (EE) is a critical quality attribute of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-RNA formulations, determining the fraction of active RNA payload available for delivery and influencing therapeutic potency, dose accuracy, and product consistency. Conventional fluorescence-based EE assays, such as RiboGreen (RG), require detergent-mediated LNP lysis, which can introduce systematic bias arising from incomplete particle disruption and additional sample handling steps. Here, we report a lysis-free method for direct EE determination using Scatter-Free Absorption Spectroscopy (SFAS) within an integrating sphere. In this approach, RG fluorescence appears as a quantitative negative absorbance feature in the SFAS spectrum, enabling direct quantification of free RNA from intact LNP suspensions in a single measurement. Applied to SM-102 LNPs loaded with polyA or mRNA in PBS or Tris/sucrose buffers, the method yielded EE in close agreement with conventional plate-reader measurements. This approach provides a practical, formulation-independent, and potentially more robust strategy for standardized routine EE analysis and LNP quality-control workflows.

abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic, whole-joint disorder marked by progressive cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodeling, synovial inflammation, and capsular fibrosis, affecting over 500 million individuals worldwide. Current pharmacotherapies are mainly palliative, with no approved disease-modifying osteoarthritis drugs (DMOADs). Intra-articular (IA) injection provides direct joint access but is hampered by rapid drug clearance and short residence times. Injectable liposome-microsphere (iLMP) systems have recently emerged as integrative delivery platforms that synergistically combine the high loading capacity, targeting versatility, and stimuli-responsiveness of liposomes with the sustained release, lubrication, mechanical support, and protective shielding of hydrogel microspheres. This "nano-in-micro" hierarchical architecture enables prolonged joint retention, spatiotemporally controlled drug release, active cell/tissue targeting, and even gene editing, thereby shifting OA management from symptom alleviation toward true disease modification. In this review, we systematically examine the rational design of iLMPs, covering liposomal composition and functionalization, microsphere fabrication technologies (microfluidics, electrospraying, 3D bioprinting, emulsification), and assembly strategies (embedding, anchoring, adsorption, and matrix hybridization). We then detail their physicochemical determinants-size, surface charge, rheology, and degradation kinetics-and discuss the multifaceted therapeutic mechanisms, including sustained pharmacokinetic modulation, boundary lubrication, active/passive targeting, enzyme/ROS/pH-responsive release, nucleic acid delivery, and exosome-hybrid biofunctionalization. Finally, we critically analyze current translational barriers (scale-up, long-term stability, safety, and cost) and outline future directions toward intelligent, personalized, and combination regimens. With continued advances in biomaterials, microengineering, and precision medicine, iLMPs are poised to become a cornerstone of next-generation OA therapy.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.

title: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer.

abstract: Developing new cancer therapeutic strategies has become a central focus in precision oncology. However, a major challenge is the lack of robust models to accurately assess target vulnerability in patient-specific heterogeneous cancer cells, which limits the translation of research findings into effective clinical therapies. In this study, we developed an ex vivo blood-based model utilizing a versatile nano-delivery platform to evaluate the responsiveness of MDM2 knockout as a representative therapeutic approach in circulating malignant cells (CMCs) from patients stratified by their p53 status. In our genome editing plasmid delivery system (p@RPA), protamine sulfate was combined with a cell-penetrating peptide to condense the CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid into nano-cores. These nano-cores were then coated with chondroitin sulfate shells functionalized with the AS1411 aptamer, enabling the selective recognition of CD44 and/or nucleolin overexpressing malignant cells. Using the same vector, a molecular beacon delivery system (MBs@RPA) co-loaded with MBMDM2 for probing MDM2 mRNA, MBTP53 for probing TP53 mRNA and MBTP73 for probing TP73 mRNA was constructed for the in situ evaluation of biomarker changes induced by genome editing. p@RPA demonstrates satisfactory efficacy in mediating gene editing for MDM2 knockout in malignant cells. Notably, the knockout of MDM2 induces cell cycle arrest and leads to a marked upregulation of anti-tumor TAp73 irrespective of their p53 status. With efficient gene editing and mRNA probing achieved in patient-derived CMCs, we establish an ex vivo platform capable of in situ therapeutic efficacy assessment at single-cell resolution to explicitly reveal the underlying cellular heterogeneity across individual CMCs.

title: A targeting delivery platform for the mapping of responses to p53-independent intervention in heterogeneous patient cancer cells.

abstract: Telomeres are essential for maintaining linear chromosome integrity, making their dysregulation in cancer an attractive target for DNA damage-mediated therapeutic interventions. Here, we explored the effects of targeting telomeric repeat sequences with CRISPR-Cas9 in human cells. At high expression levels achieved through transient transfection, telomere-specific CRISPR-Cas9 (TelCR), one of two possible telomere-targeting CRISPR-Cas9 constructs, triggered acute telomere loss, activated the ATR-CHK1/2-WEE1 G2 DNA damage checkpoint, and promoted apoptosis in HeLa cells. Conversely, an inducible system delivering sublethal levels of TelCR resulted in progressive telomere attrition and an ATM-dependent DNA damage response. TelCR also induced chromosomal instability, characterized by the formation of multicentric chromosomes. Moreover, sublethal telomeric damage elicited a transcriptional program distinct from nonspecific DNA breaks, characterized by enrichment of pathways associated with metabolic adaptation, stress responses, and innate immune signaling. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct cellular and transcriptional responses to telomere-specific CRISPR-Cas9-mediated damage, highlighting its utility as a tool for inducing targeted telomeric damage.

abstract:
Background and Rationale Cytomegalovirus (CMV) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in recipients of solid organ transplantation (SOT) and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Current management relies on antiviral prophylaxis or pre-emptive therapy guided primarily by CMV-DNAemia monitoring. However, recently introduced antivirals such as letermovir and maribavir have changed the virological profile of CMV infection, highlighting limitations of DNAemia as a marker of active viral replication and increasing the need for improved resistance monitoring.

Preliminary studies suggest that CMV-RNAemia (UL21.5 mRNA) may be a more accurate marker of active viral replication and may detect viral clearance approximately 7-14 days earlier than CMV-DNAemia. In parallel, Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) may provide superior detection of antiviral resistance mutations, including low-frequency variants that cannot be identified by conventional Sanger sequencing.

Primary Objective To determine whether using CMV-RNAemia to guide discontinuation of antiviral therapy in transplant recipients can reduce treatment duration and drug-related toxicity without increasing the risk of CMV relapse, compared with the current standard based on CMV-DNAemia.

Secondary Objectives

Compare the diagnostic performance of NGS and Sanger sequencing in detecting CMV antiviral resistance mutations.

Estimate the incidence of resistant or refractory CMV infection (R/R-CMV) in transplant recipients.

Identify risk factors associated with the development of R/R-CMV according to transplant type.

Study Design This is a single-center, pragmatic, randomized controlled interventional study conducted at the IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna.

Adult transplant recipients (≥18 years) with CMV infection requiring antiviral therapy will be randomized (1:1) into two groups:

Experimental arm: antiviral therapy discontinued after two consecutive negative CMV-RNAemia results.

Control arm: antiviral therapy discontinued after two consecutive negative CMV-DNAemia results.

Patients will be followed from treatment initiation, with virological monitoring continuing during therapy and follow-up.

Population and Sample Size The study plans to enroll approximately 330 CMV infection episodes, including an estimated 10% drop-out rate, with 150 participants per study arm plus additional cases to compensate for losses.

Endpoints Primary endpoints include:

Time to treatment discontinuation. Time to viral clearance. Incidence and timing of clinically significant CMV relapse. Antiviral drug toxicity.

Secondary endpoints include:

Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value of NGS versus Sanger sequencing. Incidence of resistant/refractory CMV infection. Identification of clinical and virological risk factors for resistance.

Resistance Analysis In suspected resistant or refractory CMV infections, residual biological samples will undergo NGS analysis targeting CMV genes involved in antiviral resistance (UL97, UL54, UL56, UL89, UL27, UL51). Results will be compared with standard Sanger sequencing to assess earlier detection of resistance mutations and minor viral variants.

Expected Impact The study aims to establish CMV-RNAemia as a clinically useful marker for earlier identification of viral clearance, enabling shorter antiviral treatment and reduced toxicity. It also seeks to validate NGS-based resistance testing as a more sensitive tool for detecting emerging CMV drug resistance, ultimately supporting a more personalized approach to CMV management in transplant recipients and potentially other immunocompromised populations.

Study Duration and Funding The study is expected to last 24 months (18 months recruitment, 4 months follow-up, 2 months analysis) and is funded by the Italian Ministry of Health (Ricerca Corrente 2026, project RC-2026-2802099).

abstract:
This study examines the effects of an eye gel containing liposomal ozonated oil in middle-aged women with dry eye disease. Dry eye can cause discomfort, an unstable tear film, and inflammation of the eye surface.

The main questions are whether one week of treatment changes:

Tear film stability and other signs and symptoms of dry eye.

Markers of inflammation in cells collected from the eye surface.

Proteins involved in maintaining connections between eye surface cells.

Women with dry eye use the eye gel for one week and undergo assessments before and after treatment. These assessments include a symptom questionnaire, eye surface examinations, and collection of small samples of cells from the conjunctiva, the thin tissue covering the white of the eye.

A separate group of healthy young women undergoes one assessment without receiving treatment. Their measurements provide reference values for comparison with those of women with dry eye.

description:
This prospective, nonrandomized interventional study combines a before-and-after treatment assessment in women with dry eye disease with a separate healthy reference group.

Women aged 45-65 years with dry eye disease receive a commercially available ophthalmic gel containing liposomal ozonated oil, hydroxyethylcellulose, and poloxamer 407 for one week. Clinical assessments and conjunctival impression cytology are performed at baseline and after treatment. Healthy women aged 18-30 years undergo a single assessment without treatment.

Conjunctival samples are examined using quantitative real-time PCR to assess the expression of inflammatory cytokines, matrix metalloproteinases, and MUC5AC. Immunofluorescence analysis of ZO-1 and E-cadherin is used to examine epithelial junctional organization and cell morphology.

Treatment-associated changes are assessed within the dry eye group. The healthy group provides a biological reference and does not serve as a randomized treatment comparator.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ectopic adiposity of skeletal muscle and the liver share common pathophysiological mechanisms predictive of physical disability. Here, we sought to characterize muscle and liver adiposity among Black Caribbeans, Black Americans, and White Americans and determine whether muscle and liver adiposity predict future gait speed.
METHODS: Computed tomography-derived abdominal lean muscle attenuation, intermuscular adipose tissue volume, and liver attenuation were measured in 749 Black Caribbean men ages 50-91 from the Tobago Longitudinal Study of Aging and 1061 Black and White American men and women ages 42-57 from the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study. Gait speed was measured 7-13 years later.
RESULTS: On average, Black Caribbean men had lean muscle attenuation that was ≥8 Hounsfield Unit (HU) higher and intermuscular adipose tissue that was ≥11 cm3 lower than Americans (p-values<0.0001), even after adjusting for age, height, walking, smoking, alcohol, energy intake, total muscle volume, and visceral adiposity. White and Black American women had lean muscle attenuation that was ≥3 HU lower and intermuscular adipose tissue that was ≥2% more of their total muscle volume (p-values<0.0001). White American men had liver attenuation that was ≥4 HU lower (p-values<0.0002), which was explained by higher visceral adiposity. Higher lean muscle attenuation and lower intermuscular adiposity were associated with faster future gait speeds (p-values≤0.007).
CONCLUSIONS: Black Caribbean men had a more favorable muscle composition, specifically higher lean muscle attenuation and lower intermuscular adiposity; characteristics that predicted better physical performance. Identifying factors explaining less myosteatosis may indicate targets to prevent physical disability.

abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems rely on cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signaling to activate ancillary nucleases such as Csm6, which serve as core effectors in antiviral immunity. While cOA-mediated Csm6 activation has been widely harnessed for molecular diagnostics, its broader application is constrained by inherent limitations, including poor cellular permeability and susceptibility to degradation by ring nucleases. Here, we conducted a high-throughput fluorescence-based screen and identified DMPCH (7,8-dimethyl-4-phenylchroman-2-one) as a non-nucleotide allosteric activator of Thermus thermophilus (Tt) Csm6. DMPCH selectively stimulates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity by binding to the higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide-binding domain dimerization interface, leading to expansion of the catalytic pocket and remodeling of the R-X4-6-H catalytic motif. Moreover, DMPCH acts synergistically with cA4 to activate TtCsm6, enabling rapid and sensitive RNA detection in a Cas13a-Csm6 system. Cell-based assays confirm that DMPCH activates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity in live bacteria cells. When combined with DMPCH, an engineered miniCsm6 fused to pyocin S2 (PyS2) exerts potent and specific bactericidal activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Our work establishes a framework for discovering non-nucleotide activators of CRISPR-associated ribonucleases and highlights their potential as chemical tools in cell-based research and as therapeutic agents against bacterial pathogens.

abstract: RNA technology, most prominently messenger RNA (mRNA), has transformed vaccine development by enabling rapid, sequence-specific antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and transient protein expression. Its long-term significance, however, extends beyond prophylactic vaccination. This Perspective argues that mRNA should be conceptualised as a programmable therapeutic platform capable of integrating vaccination, immune modulation, and on-demand disease treatment. Current mRNA vaccines deliver predefined antigenic instructions, whereas emerging RNA systems, including self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA, sequence-engineered mRNA, and targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), may support more adaptable therapeutic functions. Such platforms could prime immunity, replace deficient proteins, encode antibodies, reprogramme immune cells, or induce antigen-specific tolerance. The concept of self-adaptive RNA-based therapeutics remains at an early stage and should not be overstated; most existing systems are programmable at the design stage rather than biologically autonomous after administration. Nonetheless, this conceptual position is no longer purely speculative: the first regulatory approval of a self-amplifying RNA vaccine and controlled-trial evidence of clinical benefit from a personalised neoantigen mRNA therapeutic in resected melanoma indicate that programmable RNA platforms are beginning to move from concept to clinical validation across both the prophylactic and therapeutic ends of the spectrum. Key challenges include tissue-specific delivery, expression control, innate immune activation, repeat dosing, safety assessment, regulatory classification, and equitable access. A self-adaptive RNA-based framework does not replace existing vaccines or biologics but extends them towards responsive, personalised, and temporally controlled therapy.

title: Programmable RNA therapeutics: converging vaccination and on-demand disease treatment via self-adaptive RNA platforms.

abstract: Conventional non-amplifying messenger RNA (mRNA) and self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) medicines generally share a core linear RNA architecture-including a 5' cap, untranslated regions, one or more open reading frames, and a poly(A) tail-and are commonly formulated with delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to enable transient intracellular expression of a target protein. Prophylactic mRNA vaccines are designed primarily to express infectious-disease antigens and generate protective immune memory, whereas mRNA therapeutics exert pharmacological effects intended to treat disease, suppress recurrence, replace proteins, modulate immunity, or deliver gene-editing enzymes. Thus, even products based on similar mRNA-LNP technology may have different regulatory classifications and evidence requirements according to their intended use and mechanism of action. The clinical and regulatory landscape has expanded beyond the first coronavirus disease 2019 vaccines to include respiratory syncytial virus and influenza mRNA vaccines, an influenza-coronavirus disease 2019 combination vaccine, an authorized saRNA vaccine, personalized cancer immunotherapies, protein-replacement therapies, in vivo cell programming, and gene-editing delivery systems. This review examines which prophylactic-vaccine evidence can support therapeutic development and where product-specific quality, nonclinical, clinical, and lifecycle evidence remains necessary. For prophylactic mRNA vaccines, major regulatory considerations include quality, immunogenicity, preventive efficacy, lot release, and safety surveillance after large-scale vaccination. For mRNA therapeutics, the principal issues include delivery to target tissues, function of the expressed product, repeat-dose safety, biodistribution, off-target risk, long-term follow-up, and patient-specific manufacture and traceability. In particular, although personalized mRNA cancer vaccines are commonly described as vaccines, they are closer in regulatory purpose to therapeutics that act on the basis of each patient's tumor characteristics than to vaccines that prevent infectious disease. Antigen-selection algorithms, patient-specific sequence design, small-batch and multi-product manufacture, product-patient matching, clinical evaluation of combination strategies, manufacturing delays and analysis populations, and risk-based long-term postauthorization follow-up therefore require explicit regulatory consideration. Platform-level knowledge from prophylactic mRNA vaccine authorization can support therapeutic development, but regulatory questions may vary with each new product type; developers will need to track evolving regulatory instruments across jurisdictions and engage regulatory authorities early.

abstract: This is a phase IIb/III, double-blind, randomised, active-controlled, multi-centre, non-inferiority clinical trial that aims to determine safety, tolerability and immunogenicity of a booster vaccination with a recombinant protein receptor binding domain (RBD) fusion homodimer of XBB.1.16 adapted candidate against SARS-CoV-2 developed by HIPRA (PHH-1V81).
description:
This is a phase IIb/III, double-blind, randomised, active-controlled, multi-centre, non-inferiority clinical trial that aims to determine safety, tolerability and immunogenicity of a booster vaccination with a recombinant protein receptor binding domain (RBD) fusion homodimer of XBB.1.16 adapted candidate against SARS-CoV-2 developed by HIPRA (PHH-1V81).

Approximately 612 participants who have received a primary scheme with an EU-approved mRNA vaccine (two doses) and at least one booster dose of an EU-approved mRNA vaccine against COVID-19, will be randomly assigned to the following two treatment arms in a PHH-1V81 : Comirnaty (Omicron XBB.1.5) 2:1 ratio:

* PHH-1V81 vaccine arm: Approximately 408 adults will receive a booster dose of PHH-1V81 (HIPRA adapted vaccine).
* Comirnaty vaccine arm: Approximately 204 adults will receive a booster dose of Comirnaty Omicron XBB.1.5.

Participants will be stratified before randomisation by age group (approximately 10% of adults ≥60 years old), and by number of doses previously received.

All participants will receive a booster dose of PHH-1V81 or Comirnaty Omicron XBB.1.5 at Day 0 and will be followed for 6 months. All subjects will be closely observed for 15 minutes after vaccination on site.

abstract: Plasmodium infections and subsequent malaria disease remain a global health scourge. Liver-resident and circulating memory CD8 T cells elicited by whole parasite vaccines such as genetically or radiation-attenuated sporozoites can provide potent immunity to Plasmodium infection and prevent the development of the symptomatic blood stage of infection in humans, nonhuman primates, and mice. However, this requires multiple, large doses of attenuated sporozoites, posing numerous logistical challenges. To partially address these logistical challenges, here, we prime CB6F1 mice with a human weight-normalized, subprotective single dose of genetically or radiation-attenuated Plasmodium berghei sporozoites to elicit liver-resident and circulating memory T cells prior to boosting with a novel lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccine encoding multiple CD8 T-cell epitopes from liver-stage proteins. We show that boosting primed mice with this mRNA vaccine engenders sterilizing immunity against sporozoite challenge by generating a robust liver-stage-specific CD8 T-cell response when administered intravascularly or intramuscularly. Thus, combining a single, dose-sparing attenuated sporozoite immunization with a multi-epitope translationally relevant mRNA vaccine can engender protective immunity against P. berghei sporozoite challenge via the generation of a potent circulating and resident memory liver CD8 T-cell response. Minimizing the number of attenuated sporozoite doses required to prime CD8 T cells with a full complement of liver-stage malaria-specific epitopes effectively mitigates some logistical challenges associated with attenuated sporozoite vaccination.

abstract: Genetic epilepsy, for which the molecular mechanisms are relatively well defined in numerous monogenic forms, represents an attractive model for the transition from symptomatic seizure control to mechanism‑driven correction. However, gene therapy strategies differ in their mechanisms of action, adaptability to specific mutations and translational maturity, making rational selection of interventions based on variant‑specific functional consequences an important clinical challenge. The present review examined five nucleic acid‑based therapeutic strategies, namely gene supplementation, enhancement of endogenous gene expression, gene silencing, DNA editing and RNA editing, for major causative genes, using mutation‑specific functional consequences [loss‑of‑function (LOF) vs. gain‑of‑function] as the primary framework for therapeutic decision‑making. The mechanisms and suitability of each approach are analysed, and their performance in terms of cell‑type specificity, delivery vectors and safety is evaluated by integrating evidence from animal models, induced pluripotent stem cell‑derived neurons and organoids and clinical trials. The present review also summarised key translational barriers, including vector cargo constraints, blood‑brain barrier penetration, off‑target and immune‑associated risks, therapeutic dosing windows and the timing of developmental intervention. Antisense oligonucleotides and regulatory adeno‑associated viral approaches, supported by mature delivery platforms and manageable safety profiles, have progressed furthest towards clinical validation. Endogenous gene activation strategies, such as CRISPR activation, offer a gene replacement‑free approach for LOF disorders but remain preclinical. DNA and RNA editing, while potentially capable of durable disease modification, require further evidence on delivery efficiency and long‑term homeostatic safety. Gene therapy for genetic epilepsy is undergoing a key transition from proof‑of‑concept studies to individualised clinical application. Future progress will depend on integrating personalised intervention design, multi‑target therapeutic combinations, artificial intelligence‑assisted sequence optimisation and standardised translational models, with the potential to drive a paradigm shift from seizure suppression to mechanistic correction.

abstract: Helper lipids are essential structural components of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), yet systematic design principles linking helper lipid architecture to messenger RNA (mRNA) delivery performance remain poorly defined. Here we identify helper lipid architecture as a major, largely unexplored design lever for optimizing LNP performance. Using a modular library of more than 80 rationally designed helper lipids, we show that systematic variation in headgroup chemistry, linker topology, and tail cardinality reshapes both LNP biophysical behavior and biological performance. Martini molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with multimodal structural analyses reveal that high-performing scaffolds undergo a pH-dependent transition into fusogenic inverse hexagonal-like ordering, substantially lowering the energetic barrier for endosomal escape. These performance gains persist across the clinically relevant ALC-0315 and DLin-MC3-DMA platforms, establishing helper lipid architecture as a transferable design parameter across distinct ionizable lipid chemistries. Translating these design principles into function, optimized helper lipid formulations restore hepatic protein expression in a mouse model of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency and increase antigen expression and immunogenicity in both preclinical models and in the in vitro human MIMIC platform. Together, these findings establish helper lipids as tunable molecular actuators of potency, tolerability, and stability, offering an engineering framework for next-generation mRNA vaccines and therapeutics.

title: Engineering Tunable Helper Lipid Architecture to Improve Messenger RNA Lipid Nanoparticle Performance.

abstract: Nucleic acid-targeting technologies based on CRISPR-Cas or small-hairpin RNA (shRNA) are essential for functional genomics and therapeutic development, yet a delivery platform that simultaneously ensures high efficiency, safety, modularity, and broad cell compatibility remains lacking. Here, we report L-VLP, a virus-like particle platform derived from a B-lymphoma-isolated strain of parainfluenza virus PIV5-L. This single-cycle, replication-deficient VLP functions as a dual-mode delivery system, capable of carrying either Cas9/sgRNA for CRISPR-mediated gene editing or shRNA for RNA interference, and achieves effective target gene knockdown or knockout in both breast cancer and B-lymphoma cells. Notably, the sgRNA or shRNA cassettes in L-VLP can be readily exchanged for any sequence of interest without altering the core vector architecture, providing a modular and versatile design. Functional assays confirm that L-VLP-mediated UBR5 silencing significantly inhibits tumor cell growth in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our work establishes L-VLP as a flexible and efficient platform for manipulating gene expression, with promising applications in both basic research and cancer target therapeutics.

title: A Virus-like particle system based on parainfluenza virus PIV5-L for CRISPR-Cas9 and RNAi delivery.

abstract: Conventional cancer chemotherapy is frequently compromised by nonspecific biodistribution, dose-limiting systemic toxicity, inadequate tumor accumulation, and multidrug resistance, highlighting the need for targeted nanomedicines capable of improving tumor selectivity while preserving therapeutic efficacy. The AS1411 G-quadruplex DNA aptamer has emerged as a promising targeting ligand owing to its high affinity for nucleolin, which is aberrantly overexpressed on the surface of many malignant cells. AS1411-functionalized nanocarriers can exploit nucleolin-mediated endocytosis to enhance tumor-cell uptake, intracellular drug delivery, and therapeutic selectivity while minimizing off-target exposure. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in AS1411-engineered nanocarriers, encompassing polymeric nanoparticles, micelles, liposomes, inorganic and mesoporous nanostructures, as well as bioinspired platforms such as exosomes and cell membrane-coated nanoparticles. Particular emphasis is placed on rational nanocarrier engineering, including optimization of AS1411 surface density, PEGylation, physicochemical properties, and integration of tumor microenvironment-responsive mechanisms to achieve controlled and stimuli-responsive payload release. These platforms have been explored for the targeted delivery of conventional chemotherapeutics, nucleic acid therapeutics, and nonviral CRISPR/Cas systems, and increasingly incorporate multimodal therapeutic and diagnostic functions, including photothermal, photodynamic, sonodynamic, chemodynamic, and imaging-guided approaches. Despite considerable progress, clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous nucleolin expression, complex tumor microenvironmental barriers, limited endosomal escape and intracellular trafficking, potential off-target interactions, formulation stability, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory challenges. Future development should prioritize mechanistic understanding of AS1411-nucleolin interactions, standardized evaluation of targeting efficiency, and rational integration of multi-responsive, dual- and multi-ligand, and bioinspired architectures. Such advances may improve the translational potential of AS1411-based nanomedicines and support their further preclinical development.

title: AS1411-targeted nanomedicines for precision cancer therapy: Advances, mechanisms, and translational perspectives.

abstract: RNA modifications are being investigated as contributors to multiple myeloma (MM) biology alongside genomic lesions and bone marrow interactions. This narrative review examines N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A), 5-methylcytosine (m⁵C), adenosine-to-inosine editing, and pseudouridylation, with emphasis on the distinction between MM-specific findings and mechanisms proposed from other systems. Functional studies in MM cells and animal models link METTL3, WTAP, FTO, ALKBH5, and YTHDF2 to selected growth, metabolic, and treatment-response programs. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) has been implicated in GLI1 editing and regulation of double-stranded RNA sensing during lenalidomide exposure. Patient expression and outcome associations support clinical relevance but do not establish that these regulators determine disease behavior. Evidence for m⁵C is more limited, including an NSUN2-exosomal MALAT1 mechanism in myeloma bone disease, while the pseudouridylation studies discussed here largely concern non-myeloma cancers. Stage-specific regulatory changes across precursor disease and relapse remain hypotheses requiring longitudinal testing. Therapeutic approaches include enzyme inhibition, targeted protein degradation, and RNA-directed strategies; most remain preclinical, and several have been evaluated mainly outside MM. Plasma cell-free RNA studies provide early diagnostic observations, but modification-aware liquid biopsy has not been clinically validated for MM risk stratification, treatment selection, or relapse prediction. Progress will depend on disease-specific target validation, selective delivery, assessment of normal hematopoietic effects, and prospective clinical studies. Epitranscriptomic regulation therefore offers a useful research framework for understanding and potentially targeting MM, without displacing the established contribution of genomic and clinical risk factors.

title: Epitranscriptomic regulation contributes to multiple myeloma biology and offers potential therapeutic targets.

abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 95% of the global population and contributes to multiple human cancers and autoimmune diseases. Co-infection with pathogens including Helicobacter pylori, human immunodeficiency virus, human papillomavirus, and Plasmodium falciparum can reshape host immunity and the EBV latency-lytic balance and, in some settings, promote reactivation. Collectively, these interactions may exacerbate chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, and epigenetic dysregulation to accelerate disease progression and tumor formation. Existing clinical treatments control only the active pathogens but fail to target latent EBV. Emerging strategies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) gene editing and EBV-targeted immunotherapy aim to eliminate latent viral reservoirs. This review outlines the synergistic mechanisms of EBV co-infection in oncogenesis, highlighting that further research on pathogen interactions is vital for developing better prevention and treatment options.

title: A multipathogen view of Epstein-Barr virus pathogenesis and tumorigenesis.

abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.

abstract: Targeted protein degradation has shown powerful capability for diseases treatment. However, the approach is limited by the challenges in cellular internalization of synthetic degrader and potential cytotoxicity. Herein, we propose a Genetically encoded circular RNA Aptamer-based DEgrader (GRADE) to control target proteins degradation. The GRADE system is facilely constructed by integrating a transferrin receptor (TfR1) aptamer and target protein aptamer for delivering target protein into damaged endosomes and TfR1 binding, leading to target protein degradation via endosomal autophagy pathways. We show that the versatile and modular GRADE could be applied to eliminate several intracellular target proteins. Moreover, the GRADE system can be selectively activated by endogenous biomarkers for achieving highly specific protein degradation and cancer cell precise inhibition. This study presents a non-invasive, effective and general platform for intracellular protein degradation, offering new insights into controlled cell manipulation and diseases therapy.

title: Genetically Encoded Engineering Switchable Circular RNA Devices for Targeted Protein Degradation.

abstract: Hearing loss is among the most common sensory impairments globally and remains a significant unmet clinical challenge. Current rehabilitative approaches, such as hearing aids and cochlear implants, provide partial functional compensation but fail to restore the structural and physiological integrity of the cochlea. This review summarizes progress in therapeutic development targeting key deafness-associated genes, including OTOF, GJB2, and SLC26A4, highlighting the rationale, current clinical evidence, and major translational challenges. We further discuss the potential of combining gene therapy with stem cell-based approaches to promote inner ear regeneration and restore sensorineural function. Emerging technologies such as CRISPR/Cas, adeno-associated virus, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived otic progenitors have opened new avenues for causal correction and tissue reconstruction. Integrated therapeutic models that combine gene or stem cell therapy with cochlear implants are reshaping the treatment paradigm from symptom management to biological repair. Advances in gene editing, gene delivery, and stem cell technologies are establishing these approaches as promising treatments for hereditary hearing loss, with ongoing progress expected to accelerate clinical translation despite remaining challenges in delivery efficiency, immune responses, ethics, and long-term efficacy. Collectively, these advances mark a pivotal step toward personalized and regenerative interventions for hereditary hearing loss.

title: Emerging gene and stem cell therapies for hereditary hearing loss: from molecular correction to regenerative reconstruction.

abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality despite major advances in pharmacological therapy, interventional cardiology, and lifestyle-based prevention. Although many current treatments reduce disease burden and improve outcomes, they often fail to address the underlying molecular and genetic mechanisms driving disease progression dot CRISPR hyphen-based gene- editing systems (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) have introduced the possibility of directly correcting, silencing, or modulating pathogenic genetic determinants involved in cardiovascular pathology. When integrated with artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled design, prediction, and optimization tools, an AI-guided CRISPR framework may assist in prioritizing editing strategies, predicting editing outcomes, and informing delivery design, although cardiovascular-specific validation of these applications remains limited. This narrative review examines the potential role of AI-guided CRISPR technologies in cardiovascular disease. It first outlines the major pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying CVD, then reviews molecular and genetic targets that may be amenable to editing. Current CRISPR applications in cardiometabolic and cardiovascular disorders are discussed, followed by an evaluation of how AI may support guide RNA design, off-target prediction, vector engineering, and therapeutic prioritization. Finally, major translational barriers are examined, including tissue-specific delivery, editing in non-dividing cells, long-term genomic safety, disease complexity, and regulatory implementation. Although early preclinical findings are encouraging, most cardiovascular applications remain in the experimental or early translational stage, and direct evidence for integrated AI-guided CRISPR applications in cardiovascular disease remains limited and largely preclinical. Progress in this field will depend on advances in delivery science, genome engineering, computational modelling, and long-term safety validation. AI-guided CRISPR should therefore be regarded as a developing precision medicine strategy with substantial future potential rather than an immediately deployable clinical solution.

abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.

abstract: Here, we present a CRISPR-Cas9 protocol for generating both small indels and multi-kilobase deletions to enable genome editing in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We describe steps for a ribonucleoprotein (RNP)-based approach that integrates guide RNA selection, electroporation, and multi-tiered screening to accurately identify indels, deletions, inversions, and mixed genotypes. Human iPSCs provide a versatile genome editing platform due to their capacity for clonal expansion and differentiation. This protocol provides a scalable framework for genome editing and quality control. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Hamerlinck et al.1.

abstract: Identifying genes associated with the mechanism of action (MOA) of anticancer therapies is essential for understanding drug response. Functional genomics approaches, including genome-wide CRISPR knock out screens, enable systematic gene prioritization following treatment; however, findings from individual datasets are typically interpreted after identifying overlapping genes across datasets to confirm biological hypotheses. Integrating such heterogeneous datasets remains challenging due to variability across experimental conditions. Existing approaches can miss biologically relevant genes due to dataset-specific noise, can fail to capture genes exhibiting consistent but moderate effects across studies. Here, we present ConcuRx, a statistical framework for cross-study integration and gene prioritization across heterogeneous CRISPR drug-response screens. This approach produces more stable gene rankings than single-dataset analyses, improving prioritization of known MOA-associated genes and recovering biologically relevant genes that are overlooked by average- and overlap-based approaches. Applied to CRISPR drug-response screens for the synergistic drug pair of ATR and PARP inhibitors, ConcuRx strengthened support for 15 experimentally validated hypotheses collected from published studies, including mechanisms supported by independent studies not included in the ConcuRx analysis. These findings demonstrate that modelling between-study variability improves identification and prioritization of MOA-associated genes and provides a robust strategy for integrating heterogeneous functional genomics data in precision oncology.
